column9: stem
column15: option_b
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: The microscope in our classroom is a compound light microscope. What does the word compound mean in its name?
column14: It is built from several kinds of metal and glass joined together
column15: Light passes through the specimen and then through two lenses
column16: It can only be used on living things
column17: It shows the specimen in 3-D, so you can see its front and back at once
column28: Compound means the light goes through the specimen and then through two lenses, the objective lens and the ocular lens. A common mistake is thinking compound has to do with what the microscope is made of.
column29: Think about how many lenses the light passes through before it reaches your eye.

column9: The prefix micro- means small, and -scope means to look at. What does the word microscope mean?
column15: To measure the small
column28: Microscope means "to view the tiny," because it is used to look at things too small to see well with your eyes alone. Students sometimes pick "measure," but -scope means to look, like a telescope or a periscope.
column29: Think about other -scope words, like telescope and periscope. What do you do with them?

column9: On a compound microscope, which lens sits right above the slide?
column15: Body tube
column28: The objective lenses hang from the nosepiece just above the slide, closest to the specimen. The ocular lens is at the top where your eye goes. The body tube and diaphragm are not lenses.
column29: One lens is near your eye and the other is near the object you are looking at.

column9: The ocular lens has a second, everyday name: the ___.
column28: The ocular lens is also called the eyepiece because it is the piece your eye looks into. Don't confuse it with the objective lenses, which are down near the slide.
column29: Ocular has to do with the eye. What piece does your eye go up to?

column9: Most school microscopes have three or four objective lenses on them instead of just one. Why?
column14: There are spares in case one breaks or gets scratched during a lab
column15: One is for each person in the lab group
column16: Each one has a different magnification, so you can zoom in step by step
column17: Each one makes a different color of light, so different cell parts show up
column28: The objective lenses have different powers (such as 4×, 10×, and 40×), so you can start zoomed out and work your way up to more detail. They are not spares or color filters.
column29: Look at the numbers printed on each objective. Are they the same?

column9: Which part is the heavy bottom of the microscope that supports its weight and keeps it steady?
column15: Base
column28: The base is the bottom of the microscope; it holds the weight and keeps it from tipping. The stage is the platform for the slide, which students sometimes mix up with the base.
column29: It is the same word for the bottom of a lamp or a statue.

column9: Which part connects the base to the top of the microscope and is the part you grip when you carry it?
column15: Body tube
column28: The arm connects the base to the upper parts and is the handle for carrying. The body tube holds the lenses apart, the nosepiece holds the objectives, and the stage holds the slide. Never carry a microscope by the body tube or eyepiece.
column29: Think of the part of your body you would use to hold something up.

column9: Ana is looking at a slide on the 10× objective. She wants to switch to the 40× objective. Which part does she turn?
column15: The diaphragm
column28: The revolving nosepiece holds the objective lenses and turns (clicks) to swap one for another. A common mistake is reaching for a focus knob; the knobs move the stage, they don't change lenses.
column29: Which part do the objective lenses screw into?

column9: What is the job of the body tube?
column14: It controls how much light passes up through the slide and into the lenses
column15: It holds the slide in place
column16: It holds the ocular lens the right distance above the objective lenses
column17: It moves the stage up and down
column28: The body tube is the tube between the eyepiece and the nosepiece. It keeps the two lenses the proper distance apart so the image forms correctly. Light is controlled by the diaphragm, and the stage clips hold the slide.
column29: It is a tube. What is at each end of it?

column9: Light from the lamp shines up through a small hole in the middle of the ___, which is where you place the slide.
column28: The slide sits on the stage, and light comes up through the hole in its center. Students sometimes write "base," but the base is the bottom of the whole microscope.
column29: It is the same word for the platform a band plays on.

column9: Every time someone bumps the lab table, Leo's slide slides out of place. What should he use to keep it still?
column15: The stage clips
column28: Stage clips press down on the slide so it doesn't slide around on the stage. The diaphragm controls light, the nosepiece switches lenses, and the fine knob focuses.
column29: Which part grips the slide, like a paper clip grips paper?

column9: Some older microscopes have no lamp. What do they use to get light up through the specimen?
column14: A mirror that reflects room light up through the stage
column15: A second ocular lens
column16: A magnifying glass on the stage
column17: A flashlight built into the arm
column28: Older microscopes use a mirror under the stage. You tilt it to bounce light from a window or the room up through the specimen. A magnifying glass or extra lens would not add light.
column29: What could you tilt to bounce light where you want it?

column9: Which knob moves the stage up and down in big, fast steps?
column15: Diaphragm lever
column28: The coarse adjustment knob is the larger knob. It moves the stage a lot with each turn, which is why it is only used on low power. The fine knob makes tiny moves.
column29: Coarse sand has big grains. Which knob makes big moves?

column9: Which knob moves the stage only a tiny amount, so you can sharpen an image that is already almost in focus?
column15: Stage clip
column28: The fine adjustment knob makes small, precise moves to sharpen the image. It is the only focus knob to use on high power. The coarse knob makes big moves.
column29: Fine can mean thin or delicate. Which knob makes delicate moves?

column9: Match each microscope part to where you find it on the microscope.
column14: Ocular lens :: At the very top of the microscope
column15: Revolving nosepiece :: Just below the body tube
column16: Coarse adjustment knob :: On the side of the arm
column18: Light source :: Built into the base
column28: From top to bottom: ocular lens, body tube, revolving nosepiece with the objectives, stage, diaphragm just under the stage, and the light source in the base. The focus knobs are on the side of the arm. A common mix-up is putting the diaphragm above the stage; it sits below, between the light and the slide.
column29: Picture light traveling from the bottom of the microscope up to your eye.

column9: To find the total magnification of a compound microscope, what do you do with the power of the ocular lens and the power of the objective lens?
column15: Multiply them
column28: Total magnification = ocular power × objective power. The most common mistake is adding the two numbers.
column29: Each lens enlarges the image made by the one before it. Is that adding or multiplying?

column9: A microscope has a 15× ocular lens, and its 4× objective lens is clicked into place. What is the total magnification? Type just the number.
column28: Total magnification = 15 × 4 = 60, so the specimen looks 60 times larger. Adding (15 + 4 = 19) is the common mistake.
column29: Multiply the ocular power by the objective power.

column9: Sam's microscope has a 10× eyepiece. He clicks the 10× objective into place. What is the total magnification? Type just the number.
column28: Total magnification = 10 × 10 = 100. Adding the two lenses would give 20, which is the common mistake.
column29: Eyepiece power times objective power.

column9: A microscope at a nature center has a 5× ocular lens and a 40× objective lens. What is the total magnification? Type just the number.
column28: Total magnification = 5 × 40 = 200. Don't add (45) and don't just report the objective (40).
column29: Multiply the two lens powers.

column9: What should you use to clean a dirty microscope lens?
column15: A paper towel
column28: Use lens paper (a soft lens tissue). Paper towels and clothing can scratch the glass, and fingers leave oily smudges that make the image blurry.
column29: Pick the choice made especially for delicate glass.

column9: Where should a microscope sit while you are using it?
column14: On your lap so it is close to your eyes
column15: Right at the edge of the table so it is closer to you
column16: On top of a textbook to raise it up
column17: On a flat, steady table, away from the edge
column28: A microscope should sit flat on a steady table, away from the edge, so it can't tip or get knocked off. Laps, table edges, and stacks of books are all unsteady.
column29: Which spot would keep it from tipping or getting knocked over?

column9: On most microscopes, the higher-power objective lenses are longer than the low-power objective lenses.
column28: True. The 4× objective is the shortest, and the 40× is much longer. That is why the 40× lens ends up very close to the slide and why you must be careful when focusing on high power.
column29: Picture which objective ends up almost touching the slide.

column9: At the end of class, which objective should be clicked into place before you put the microscope away?
column15: The 40× objective
column28: Put the microscope away on the lowest-power (shortest) objective. It sits farthest from the stage, so it is least likely to get bumped or scratched, and the next person starts in the right place.
column29: Which objective is the shortest and safest to leave down?

column9: A jeweler checks a diamond by holding a single lens, like a magnifying glass, up to it. What type of microscope is this?
column15: Simple microscope
column28: A simple microscope has only one lens, like a magnifying glass or a jeweler's loupe. A compound microscope uses two lenses, a stereoscopic microscope gives a 3-D view, and an electron microscope uses electrons.
column29: Count the lenses. How many is the jeweler using?

column9: A medical lab spreads a very thin smear of blood on a glass slide so light can shine through it. The technician wants to count the blood cells. Which microscope fits this job?
column15: Simple magnifying glass
column17: No microscope; cells can be counted by eye
column28: Blood cells are far too small for a magnifying glass or the eye, and a thin smear on a slide is exactly what a compound light microscope is built for. A dissecting microscope is for looking at the outside of larger, whole objects.
column29: The specimen is thin, on a slide, and the cells are tiny. Which microscope is made for that?

column9: A scientist needs to see a virus, which is far too small for any light microscope. Which kind of microscope does she need?
column15: Compound light microscope with a brighter lamp
column28: Viruses are too small to see with light. An electron microscope uses beams of electrons bent by magnets instead of light, so it can show much smaller things. A brighter lamp does not help a light microscope see smaller objects.
column29: If light can't do the job, what does the microscope have to use instead?

column9: When you use a microscope, what is the object or sample you are looking at called?
column15: The field
column28: The specimen is whatever you are studying, such as a hair, an onion skin, or pond water. The stage is the platform it sits on, and the field of view is the circle you see.
column29: Scientists call a sample they study a ___.

column9: On a wet mount, the specimen is covered with a thin square of glass or plastic called a ___.
column28: The cover slip is the thin square placed over the specimen and the water. Students sometimes call it the slide, but the slide is the thicker glass underneath.
column29: It covers the specimen, and it is thin enough to slip over the drop.

column9: To make a wet mount, you put the specimen on a slide and add a drop of what?
column15: Water
column28: A wet mount uses a drop of water. The water keeps the specimen flat and moist and helps light pass through it evenly. Oil, glue, and sanitizer would damage the specimen or the lens.
column29: The name of the slide is a clue.

column9: What is the best way to put a cover slip onto a drop of water on a slide?
column14: Touch one edge to the slide at about a 45° angle, then slowly lower it
column15: Drop it flat from a few centimeters above so it lands evenly on the water
column16: Press it flat with your thumb
column17: Slide it in from the side, then add a drop of water on top so it spreads under
column28: Holding the cover slip at about 45° and lowering it slowly lets the water spread out and pushes air out ahead of it. Dropping it flat or pressing it traps air bubbles and can crack the glass.
column29: You want the water to spread across slowly and push the air out.

column9: A thin onion skin looks washed out and almost all white because too much light is coming through. Which part should be adjusted?
column15: The stage clips
column28: The diaphragm sits under the stage and opens or closes to control how much light reaches the specimen. Closing it a little cuts the glare. The focus knobs and stage clips do not change brightness.
column29: Which part works like the pupil of your eye, letting in more or less light?

column9: What is the field of view?
column15: The distance between the objective lens and the slide when the image is in focus
column16: The circle of the slide you can see when you look into the microscope
column17: The size of the glass slide
column28: The field of view is the bright circle you see through the eyepiece; it is the part of the slide you can see at one time. It is not the magnification or a distance.
column29: What do you actually see when you put your eye up to the eyepiece?

column9: The diaphragm stays at the same setting. How does the view change when you switch from low power to high power?
column15: It gets dimmer
column28: High power looks dimmer because the lens gathers light from a much smaller area. That is why you often need to open the diaphragm on high power. Many students guess brighter because the image is bigger.
column29: Think about spreading the same light over a much bigger image.

column9: Why should you carry a microscope upright with two hands?
column14: So it doesn't fall, and loose parts like the eyepiece don't slide out
column15: So you look more professional
column17: So you can look through it while you walk and check that the slide is still in place
column28: Carrying it upright with one hand on the arm and one under the base keeps it from slipping and keeps the eyepiece from falling out of the tube. Never look through it while walking.
column29: What could happen if it tipped or slipped while you walked?

column9: Which of these would you need a compound light microscope to see clearly?
column14: The outline of a maple leaf
column15: The stripes on a bumblebee
column17: Single cells in a thin layer of onion skin
column28: Single cells are too small to see by eye, and a thin onion layer lets light through, so a compound light microscope is perfect. A leaf outline and bee stripes are big enough to see by eye, and atoms are far too small for any light microscope.
column29: Which thing is too small for your eye but not impossibly small?

column9: Where can you find the magnification of each objective lens?
column15: Written on the stage
column16: Printed on the side of each objective lens
column28: Each objective lens has its power (such as 4×, 10×, or 40×) printed right on its side. Look there before you calculate total magnification.
column29: Look closely at the lenses themselves.

column9: Which objective lens lets you see the largest area of the slide at once?
column15: The 4× objective
column17: They all show the same area
column28: The lower the power, the bigger the field of view. The 4× lens shows the most area, and each higher power shows a smaller piece of the slide but bigger.
column29: Zooming in shows more detail. Does it show more area or less?

column9: Which of these parts are used to focus the image? Choose all that apply.
column15: Fine adjustment knob
column28: The coarse and fine adjustment knobs move the stage to focus. The diaphragm controls light, the stage clips hold the slide, and the base supports the microscope.
column29: Look for the parts with the word adjustment in their names.

column9: Which of these would work well as a wet mount specimen on a compound light microscope? Choose all that apply.
column15: A whole grape
column16: One thin layer peeled from an onion
column28: A hair, one thin onion layer, and a few cotton fibers are thin enough for light to shine through. A whole grape, a thick carrot slice, and a coin are too thick or solid, so they would just look dark.
column29: Light comes from below. Pick the things thin enough for it to shine through.

column9: Ty switched to the 40× objective, and the image is just a little blurry. He should turn the ___ adjustment knob.
column28: On high power use only the fine adjustment knob. The 40× objective is very close to the slide, and the coarse knob moves the stage so much it could crack the slide or scratch the lens.
column29: Use the knob that makes only tiny moves.

column9: What is the lowest-power objective best used for?
column14: Finding the specimen and getting an overview before zooming in
column15: Seeing tiny details inside a cell, like the parts of the nucleus
column16: Focusing with only the fine knob
column28: The lowest-power objective is where you find the specimen and see the big picture. Small details come later on high power. A common mistake is starting on high power and never finding the specimen.
column29: Before you can zoom in on something, what do you have to do first?

column9: Which of these is a prepared slide?
column14: A temporary slide you make in class with a drop of water
column15: A slide with the cover slip taken off
column16: A slide with no specimen on it
column17: A permanent slide made by a science supply company
column28: A prepared slide is permanent and is bought already made. A slide you make in class with water is a wet mount, which is temporary.
column29: Prepared means it was made ahead of time to keep.

column9: What does "40×" printed on an objective lens mean?
column14: The lens is 40 millimeters long from the nosepiece to its tip
column15: It is lens number 40 in the set
column16: It makes the specimen look 40 times larger than it really is
column17: It can be used for 40 minutes at a time before it gets too hot
column28: The × means "times." A 40× objective makes the specimen look 40 times larger. The total magnification is that number times the ocular power.
column29: The × symbol is read as "times."

column9: The zoom button on a phone camera makes things look bigger. Which microscope action does the same kind of job?
column14: Opening the diaphragm so more light comes up through the slide
column15: Switching from a low-power objective to a high-power objective
column16: Turning the coarse adjustment knob to bring the specimen closer to the lens
column28: Switching to a higher-power objective is the microscope's zoom: the image gets bigger. The diaphragm changes brightness, the coarse knob focuses, and stage clips hold the slide.
column29: Which action changes the magnification?

column9: A student wants to measure how wide the field of view is in millimeters. What should she put on the stage?
column15: A thermometer
column28: A clear ruler lets light shine through, so you can count the millimeter marks across the field of view. The other tools measure temperature, volume, and mass, not length.
column29: Which tool measures length and is clear enough for light to pass through?

column9: A student wants to view one cell on high power. Put her steps in the correct order.
column14: Watch from the side while turning the nosepiece to 40×
column15: Focus on the cell with the coarse knob on the 4× objective
column16: Look through the eyepiece and sharpen the image
column17: Move the slide so the cell is in the center of the view
column28: Focus on low power first, center the cell, watch from the side as you switch to 40× so the lens doesn't hit the slide, then sharpen the image (with the fine knob only). The common mistake is switching to high power before centering, which makes the cell disappear from the smaller view.
column29: You can't center something you haven't found yet, and sharpening comes last.

column9: Put the steps for making and viewing a wet mount in order.
column14: Put the slide on the stage with the lowest-power objective in place
column15: Add one drop of water on top of the specimen
column16: Place a thin specimen in the middle of a clean slide
column17: Gently lower the cover slip over the drop
column28: Specimen first, water on top of it, then the cover slip, and finally onto the stage on low power. Putting the cover slip on before the water, or starting on high power, are the common mistakes.
column29: The water goes on top of the specimen, and the cover slip goes on top of the water.

column9: Put these in the order that light passes through them, starting from where the light begins and ending at your eye.
column15: Specimen on the slide
column28: Light starts at the lamp, passes through the diaphragm, up through the specimen on the stage, into the objective lens, up the body tube, and out the ocular lens to your eye. Students often put the objective before the specimen, but the light must pass through the specimen first.
column29: Light starts at the bottom of the microscope and travels up to your eye.

column9: Max's older microscope has no lamp. The view goes dark every time he leans in close and blocks the window behind him. What should he do?
column15: Switch to the 40× objective so the image is bigger and easier to see
column17: Move so his body isn't blocking the light from the window
column28: Without a lamp, the microscope depends on outside light being reflected up through the specimen. If Max's body blocks that light, the view goes dark. Closing the diaphragm would make it even darker, and changing lenses or focus doesn't add light.
column29: Where is this microscope's light coming from, and what is in the way?

column9: A slide has a lowercase letter "b" on it, placed so it reads normally to you. Which letter will it look like through the microscope?
column15: p
column28: The microscope flips the image both upside down and backward, which is the same as turning it halfway around. A "b" turned halfway around looks like a "q." A "d" is only flipped left-right, and a "p" is only flipped upside down.
column29: Write a b on paper and turn the paper halfway around.

column9: While looking through the eyepiece, Jo pushes the slide away from her body. Which way does the image move in the view?
column14: Away from her (up in the view)
column15: Toward her (down in the view)
column28: The image moves in the opposite direction from the slide. When the slide moves away from you, the image moves toward you. The common mistake is expecting it to move the same way you push.
column29: The image is flipped. Does it move with your hand or against it?

column9: An amoeba is at the right edge of the field of view and creeping out of sight. Which way should you move the slide to bring it back to the center?
column15: To the left
column28: In the view, things move opposite to the slide. To make the image move left toward the center, slide the slide to the right. A quick rule: move the slide toward the side where the specimen is.
column29: The image moves opposite to the slide. Which way do you need the image to go?

column9: On the 4× objective, a microscope's total magnification is 40×. The student then switches to the 40× objective. What is the new total magnification? Type just the number.
column28: First find the ocular: 40 ÷ 4 = 10×. Then multiply by the new objective: 10 × 40 = 400. A common mistake is answering 40, which is only the objective's power.
column29: Use the first total to figure out the ocular lens power.

column9: Microscope A has a 10× ocular and a 10× objective. Microscope B has a 25× ocular and a 4× objective. Compared with microscope A, how large will the same cell look in microscope B?
column14: Larger, because B has the stronger ocular
column15: Larger, because B's numbers add up to more
column16: Smaller, because B's objective is weaker
column28: Total magnification is what matters. A: 10 × 10 = 100×. B: 25 × 4 = 100×. They are equal, so the cell looks the same size. Comparing only one lens, or adding the numbers, leads to the wrong answer.
column29: Find the total magnification of each microscope before comparing.

column9: A student wants to compare how thick a human hair and a dog hair are. Which method gives the fairest comparison?
column14: Look at the human hair on 40× and the dog hair on 400×
column15: Look at each hair on a different microscope with different lenses
column16: Look at both hairs on the same slide at the same magnification
column17: Only look at the hair that seems thicker
column28: To compare sizes fairly, keep the magnification the same, best of all side by side in the same view. Using different magnifications changes how big each one looks, which is not a fair test.
column29: In a fair test, what should stay the same?

column9: Drew's cheek cell wet mount is full of round, empty-looking rings with thick dark edges, and the cells are hard to find among them. What are the rings?
column15: Air bubbles trapped under the cover slip
column17: Drops of oil from his fingers
column28: Perfectly round, clear circles with dark outlines are air bubbles trapped under the cover slip. Lowering the cover slip slowly from about 45° pushes the air out. Students often mistake bubbles for cells, but cells are not perfect empty circles.
column29: What gets trapped under a cover slip when it is dropped flat?

column9: Why should you always start on the lowest-power objective when looking at a new slide?
column14: It is the easiest place to find the specimen, and its short lens sits far from the slide
column15: It shows more detail than any other lens
column16: It is the only objective that turns the image right side up
column17: It uses less electricity than the other objectives, so the lamp stays cool and lasts longer
column28: Low power has the widest field of view, so you can find the specimen, and the short lens sits far from the slide, so you won't crash into it. Low power shows less detail, not more, and no objective turns the image right side up.
column29: Think about both how much you can see and how close the lens is to the slide.

column9: Why should you never use the coarse adjustment knob while the 40× objective is in place?
column14: The coarse knob doesn't move anything on high power, so turning it would just waste time
column15: It would turn the image upside down
column16: It would make the light too bright
column17: The 40× lens sits very close to the slide, so a big move could crash the lens into it
column28: On high power the objective is only a tiny distance above the slide. The coarse knob moves the stage a lot, so it can ram the slide into the lens and break the slide or scratch the lens. It doesn't affect the light or the image's direction.
column29: How much space is there between the 40× lens and the slide?

column9: Which of these could damage a microscope or a slide? Choose all that apply.
column14: Wiping the lenses with a paper towel
column15: Opening the diaphragm all the way
column16: Setting the microscope down hard on the counter
column17: Using the fine knob on the 40× objective
column18: Carrying the microscope with one hand by the eyepiece
column19: Moving the slide while looking through the eyepiece
column28: Paper towels can scratch lenses, banging the microscope down can knock parts out of line, and carrying it by the eyepiece can drop it. Opening the diaphragm, using the fine knob on high power, and moving the slide while you look are all normal, safe actions.
column29: For each one, ask: could this scratch, bend, crack, or drop something?

column9: A slide has three colored threads crossed on top of each other. On high power, a student can get one thread sharp, but the other two are blurry. Why can't she get all three in focus at once?
column15: The light is too dim on high power to light up all three threads at once
column16: The microscope focuses on one thin layer at a time, and the threads sit at different depths
column17: High power can only focus on one object at a time, no matter how they are arranged on the slide
column28: A microscope is in focus at only one depth at a time. The threads lie on top of each other, so each is at a different height. Turning the fine knob moves the focus up or down through them. Color has nothing to do with it.
column29: The threads are stacked. Are they all the same distance from the lens?

column9: A student draws onion cells and labels her drawing "40×." She used a 10× ocular and the 40× objective. What is wrong with her label?
column15: She should record the total magnification, which is 400×
column16: Nothing; only the objective lens matters, because the ocular doesn't magnify
column28: Drawings should be labeled with the total magnification: 10 × 40 = 400×. Writing just the objective power is the most common labeling mistake, and adding the lenses (50×) is wrong too.
column29: Both lenses magnify the image.

column9: A student puts a slide on the stage, but on the 4× objective she sees only a bright, empty circle, even after turning the coarse knob through its whole range. What should she check first?
column14: That the specimen is right over the hole in the stage
column15: That the diaphragm is closed, so the light is not too bright
column17: That she is on the 40× objective, which makes the specimen easier to find
column28: If you only see an empty bright circle, the specimen is probably not over the light. Center the specimen over the stage opening first. A dirty eyepiece would add specks, not erase the specimen.
column29: If nothing at all shows up, is the specimen even in the light's path?

column9: Two students look at the same prepared slide. One sees one large cell with lots of detail. The other sees dozens of small cells. What is most likely different?
column14: The first student's slide has bigger cells
column15: The second student's light is brighter
column16: The first student turned the coarse knob more, which made the cells look bigger and clearer
column17: They are using different objective lenses; the first student is on higher power
column28: Same slide, different views: higher power shows fewer cells, larger and in more detail; lower power shows more cells, smaller. Brightness and focus don't change how many cells fit in the view.
column29: What changes both how big things look and how many fit in the view?

column9: A microscope has a 20× ocular lens. Match each objective lens to the total magnification it gives.
column15: 10× objective :: 200×
column28: Multiply each objective by the 20× ocular: 20 × 4 = 80, 20 × 10 = 200, 20 × 40 = 800, and 20 × 100 = 2,000. Adding instead of multiplying is the common mistake.
column29: Multiply each objective by 20.

column9: A student's notes say: "With a 10× ocular, switching from the 10× objective to the 40× objective made the cells look 4 times larger." Is she right?
column14: No; they look 30 times larger, since 40 minus 10 is 30
column15: No; they look 40 times larger, because the new objective is 40×
column16: Yes; the total goes from 100× to 400×, which is 4 times larger
column28: Before: 10 × 10 = 100×. After: 10 × 40 = 400×. 400 ÷ 100 = 4, so the cells look 4 times larger. Subtracting (30) or using only the new objective (40) are common mistakes.
column29: Find both total magnifications, then divide.

column9: A student is trying to see cells in a thick slice of potato, but all she sees is a dark blob. What is the best fix?
column15: Make a new wet mount with a much thinner slice
column28: A compound microscope shines light up through the specimen, so the specimen must be very thin. A thick slice blocks the light. More magnification or a faster coarse knob won't help a slice that is too thick.
column29: Where does the light come from, and can it get through a thick slice?

column9: A student has finished looking at a wet mount. What should she do before putting the microscope away?
column14: Take off the slide and dry any water on the stage
column15: Leave the slide on the stage for the next class
column16: Rinse the lenses under the faucet
column17: Dry the lenses with a paper towel
column28: Remove the slide and wipe up water so the stage doesn't rust or get sticky. Never rinse a microscope under water, and never use paper towels on lenses; use lens paper.
column29: What could happen to a metal stage if water sat on it overnight?

column9: Which of these would be best viewed with a stereoscopic (dissecting) microscope instead of a compound light microscope? Choose all that apply.
column15: Cheek cells in a thin smear
column17: Single-celled organisms in a drop of pond water
column18: The seeds on the outside of a strawberry
column28: A stereoscopic microscope gives a low-power, 3-D view of the outside of whole objects like an ant, a pinecone, or a strawberry. Cheek cells and single-celled organisms are tiny and thin, so they need a compound light microscope.
column29: Which ones are whole objects you would want to see in 3-D, and which are tiny and thin enough for light to pass through?

column9: When you draw what you see through a microscope, which is the best practice?
column14: Copy the picture from the textbook so it looks correct
column15: Draw the slide as it looks from above on the stage, not through the eyepiece, so the position is right
column16: Leave off the magnification so the drawing looks cleaner
column17: Draw only what you actually see, in the same position, and label it with the total magnification
column28: A scientific drawing records your own observation: what you saw, where it was in the view, and the total magnification you used. Copying a textbook picture or skipping the magnification makes the drawing useless as data.
column29: A drawing is a record of your observation. What would another scientist need to know?

column9: A small dot is in the lower-left corner of a slide, as you look down at it on the stage. Where will the dot appear in the field of view?
column15: Upper left
column28: The image is flipped both upside down and left-to-right. Lower becomes upper, and left becomes right, so the dot appears in the upper right. Flipping only one direction is the common mistake.
column29: Flip it top-to-bottom AND left-to-right.

column9: Why is a cover slip placed over a wet mount?
column15: It keeps the specimen flat and wet and keeps water off the objective lens
column16: It colors the specimen so the cell parts are easier to see under the light
column17: It makes the slide heavier so it won't move
column28: The cover slip flattens the specimen into one layer, slows drying, and protects the objective lens from getting wet. It does not magnify or stain anything.
column29: What might happen to the water and the lens without it?

column9: Which of these lens combinations gives the highest total magnification?
column15: 6× ocular with a 40× objective
column28: Multiply each pair: 15 × 20 = 300, 6 × 40 = 240, 20 × 4 = 80, and 25 × 10 = 250. The 15× and 20× pair is highest. Picking the pair with the single biggest number (40×), or adding, leads to the wrong choice.
column29: Multiply each pair. Don't just look for the biggest number.

column9: Four lab partners are using microscopes. Which partner is following the rules?
column14: Partner A switches to 40× and focuses with the coarse knob
column15: Partner B wipes the eyepiece with a paper towel
column16: Partner C tilts the microscope toward himself so he can see better without bending down over it
column17: Partner D starts on 4×, focuses, and centers the specimen before switching to higher power
column28: Partner D does it right: low power first, focus, center, then zoom. Using the coarse knob on 40× can crack the slide, paper towels scratch lenses, and tilting the microscope can make it fall.
column29: Look for the partner who could not break anything.

column9: At the start of class, Mia notices the 40× objective is still clicked into place from the last class. What should she do before putting her slide on the stage?
column14: Leave it, because 40× shows the most detail
column15: Lower the stage with the fine knob only
column16: Turn the nosepiece to the lowest-power objective
column28: Always begin on the lowest-power objective. It leaves room to place the slide without hitting the long 40× lens and gives you the widest view to find your specimen.
column29: Which objective do you always start on?

column9: A microscope gives 400× on high power with its 10× ocular lens. The teacher swaps in a 15× ocular lens. What is the new total magnification on high power? Type just the number.
column28: The high-power objective is 400 ÷ 10 = 40×. With the new eyepiece: 15 × 40 = 600. A common mistake is adding 5 to the old total.
column29: First figure out the high-power objective, then multiply by the new ocular.

column9: On the 10× objective, a student counts about 20 cells across the field of view. After switching to the 40× objective, about how many cells will fit across the view?
column15: About 5
column28: Going from 10× to 40× is 4 times the magnification, so the field of view becomes 4 times narrower: 20 ÷ 4 = 5 cells. The common mistake is multiplying (80), as if higher power showed more.
column29: Higher power shows less area. By what factor did the magnification go up?

column9: On the 4× objective, the field of view is 4.0 mm across. A strand of algae stretches about halfway across the field. About how long is the algae, in mm? Type just the number.
column28: Half of a 4.0 mm field is about 2 mm. Estimating with the field of view works like using a ruler you already know the length of. Don't use the magnification here; the field width is already a real distance.
column29: If the whole circle is 4.0 mm across, what is half of it?

column9: On low power (total 40×), the field of view is 5.0 mm across. What is the field of view on high power (total 400×), in mm? Type just the number.
column28: The magnification went up 10 times (40× to 400×), so the field of view gets 10 times smaller: 5.0 ÷ 10 = 0.5 mm. The common mistake is multiplying by 10 and getting 50 mm, but higher power always shows a smaller area.
column29: When magnification goes up, does the field get bigger or smaller, and by how much?

column9: On low power, the field of view is 2,000 µm across. About 8 onion cells fit end to end across the middle of the field. About how long is one onion cell, in µm? Type just the number.
column28: Divide the field width by the number of cells: 2,000 ÷ 8 = 250 µm per cell. Multiplying (16,000) is the common mistake; the cells share the field, so each is a fraction of it.
column29: The 8 cells together span the whole field. How much of it does one cell take up?

column9: Which lowercase letter would look exactly the same when viewed through a compound light microscope?
column15: e
column28: The microscope turns the image halfway around (upside down and backward). An "s" turned halfway around is still an "s." An "e" looks upside-down and backward, a "b" becomes a "q," and an "r" turns upside-down.
column29: Write each letter on paper and turn the paper halfway around.

column9: A student wants a word printed on a slide to appear in normal reading position when she looks through the eyepiece. How should she place the slide on the stage?
column15: Flipped over so the word is face down, since the lenses will flip it right side up again
column17: Turned halfway around, so the word looks upside down and backward to her from above
column28: The microscope turns the image halfway around. If the slide is already turned halfway around, the two turns cancel and the word reads normally. Flipping the slide face down would mirror the word and put glass between the lens and the specimen.
column29: Two half-turns add up to what?

column9: On the 10× objective, a paramecium is swimming toward the top of the field of view. To keep it centered, which way should you move the slide?
column14: Toward you, opposite to the way it seems to be swimming
column15: Don't move it; switch to 40× instead so it is easier to keep in view
column16: Away from you, in the same direction it seems to be swimming
column28: The image moves opposite to the slide. The paramecium is drifting up in the view, so you need the image to move back down, which means pushing the slide away from you. The rule: move the slide toward where the specimen is heading. Switching to 40× would make it leave the smaller view even faster.
column29: Moving the slide away from you makes the image move which way?

column9: A slide has three crossed threads: blue on the bottom, red in the middle, and yellow on top. Watching from the side, a student raises the stage until it is close to the 10× objective and none of the threads is in focus. She then looks through the eyepiece and slowly lowers the stage. Which thread comes into focus first?
column15: Blue, the bottom thread
column17: All three at the same time
column28: The lens is sharp at one set distance below it. With the stage raised close, all three threads sit above that point. As the stage goes down, the lowest thread reaches it first, so blue focuses first, then red, then yellow. Many students pick the top thread because it is closest to the lens.
column29: With the stage close, the in-focus spot is below all three threads. Which thread reaches that spot first as the stage drops?

column9: A student focuses a slide fine on the 4× and 10× objectives. On 40×, she can't get it in focus no matter how she turns the fine knob, and the lens almost touches the glass. What is the most likely cause?
column14: The slide is upside down, so the specimen is under the thick slide glass
column15: The diaphragm is open too wide, so too much light washes out the image on 40×
column17: The stage clips are too loose
column28: The 40× lens has to get very close to the specimen. If the slide is upside down, the specimen is under the slide glass, too far away for the 40× lens to reach. Low power still works because those lenses focus from farther away. Light and dirt don't stop focusing completely.
column29: What is between the 40× lens and the specimen if the slide is flipped over?

column9: A student says, "The 40× objective is better than the 4× objective for every job." Which is the best response?
column14: Yes, more magnification is always better, since you can see more of each cell
column15: Yes, as long as you use the coarse knob
column16: No, the 4× objective is better for every job, because it shows the most of the slide
column17: No. Different jobs need different lenses, so neither one is best for everything
column28: Neither lens is best for everything. You need low power to find the specimen and see how parts fit together, and high power to see fine detail. Thinking more magnification is always better is a common misconception.
column29: Could you find a tiny specimen on a big slide using only high power?

column9: A microscope has a 10× ocular and objectives of 4×, 10×, and 40×. How many times larger does the specimen look on the highest power than on the lowest power? Type just the number.
column28: Lowest total: 10 × 4 = 40×. Highest total: 10 × 40 = 400×. 400 ÷ 40 = 10 times larger. Subtracting (360) answers a different question; "how many times" means divide.
column29: Find both totals. "How many times larger" means divide.

column9: Put these lens combinations in order from the lowest total magnification to the highest.
column15: 25× ocular with a 4× objective
column28: Multiply each pair: 25 × 4 = 100, 10 × 20 = 200, 20 × 15 = 300, and 5 × 100 = 500. Judging by the biggest single number or by adding gives the wrong order.
column29: Find each total magnification first, then order them.

column9: At 40× total, an organism stretches across about 1/10 of the field of view. The student switches to 400× total and keeps it centered. About how much of the field will it fill now?
column15: About 1/10 of the field
column16: The whole width of the field
column28: The image gets 10 times bigger (40× to 400×), and the field of view gets 10 times narrower. Something that was 1/10 of the width is now 10/10, the whole width. Thinking the organism stays the same fraction, or gets smaller, is the common mistake.
column29: If the image gets 10 times bigger, what happens to 1/10?

column9: Which wet mount will give the clearest view of cheek cells?
column14: A thick clump of cells with five drops of water and no cover slip
column15: A thin smear of cells, one drop of water, and a cover slip set down gently
column16: A thin smear with a cover slip pressed down hard with a thumb
column17: A thick clump with a cover slip dropped flat from above
column28: Clear views need a thin layer (so light passes), the right amount of water, and a cover slip set down gently (no bubbles). Thick clumps block light, extra water floods the slide, and pressing or dropping the cover slip traps bubbles or cracks the glass.
column29: Look for the choice where every step is done carefully.

column9: On high power, the field of view is 450 µm across. A yeast cell is about 5 µm wide. About how many yeast cells could fit side by side across the field? Type just the number.
column28: Divide the field width by the width of one cell: 450 ÷ 5 = 90 cells. Multiplying (2,250) is the common mistake; you are asking how many 5s fit into 450.
column29: How many 5 µm pieces fit into 450 µm?

column9: A dark speck shows up in the view. Match each observation to where the speck must be.
column14: The speck moves when you move the slide :: On the slide
column15: The speck stays put when you move the slide but disappears when you switch objectives :: On the objective lens
column16: The speck stays put when you move the slide and when you switch objectives :: On the ocular lens
column28: If it moves with the slide, it is on the slide. If it stays when the slide moves but leaves when you change objectives, it was on that objective. If it stays through both tests, the only thing that hasn't changed is the eyepiece, so it's on the ocular lens.
column29: Test one thing at a time: what changed, and did the speck go with it?

column9: With a 10× ocular, a microscope's field of view is 4.5 mm on the 4× objective, 1.8 mm on the 10× objective, and 0.45 mm on the 40× objective. A cell is about 0.1 mm across. On which objective will the cell take up about a quarter of the width of the field?
column15: 4× objective
column28: Divide the cell size by each field: 0.1 ÷ 4.5 ≈ 1/45, 0.1 ÷ 1.8 ≈ 1/18, and 0.1 ÷ 0.45 ≈ 1/4.5, about a quarter. Only the 40× objective makes it fill that much of the view. A common mistake is thinking the biggest field shows the cell best.
column29: For each objective, divide the cell size by the field width.

column9: A photo taken through a microscope at 400× total magnification shows a cell that measures 20 mm across in the photo. About how big is the real cell, in mm? Type just the number.
column28: The photo is 400 times bigger than real life, so the real size = image size ÷ magnification = 20 ÷ 400 = 0.05 mm. Multiplying (8,000 mm) is the common mistake; the real cell must be smaller than the picture.
column29: Is the real cell bigger or smaller than the picture? Divide by the magnification.

column9: Two lab groups estimate the length of the same cell. Group A uses the 4× objective, where the cell takes up a tiny sliver of the field. Group B uses the 40× objective, where the cell spans about half the field. Whose estimate is likely more precise, and why?
column14: Group A, because a bigger field of view shows more area, so it is always more accurate
column15: Group A, because low power has less blur
column16: Both are equally precise, because it is the same cell and its real size does not change
column17: Group B, because the cell fills more of the field, so small guessing errors matter less
column28: Estimating "half the field" is much easier and more precise than estimating a tiny sliver like "1/40 of the field." Group B's view makes the cell large enough to judge well. A bigger field shows more area, but it doesn't make size estimates better.
column29: Is it easier to judge a fraction like 1/2 or a fraction like 1/40?

column9: Halfway through observing a wet mount, the water starts drying out and air creeps in from the edges of the cover slip. What is the best fix?
column14: Lift off the cover slip and rub the specimen so it spreads into a thin layer
column15: Open the diaphragm all the way
column16: Add a drop of water at the edge of the cover slip so it seeps underneath
column28: A drop placed at the edge of the cover slip gets pulled underneath and refills the mount without disturbing the specimen. Lifting the cover slip adds more bubbles, and changing the light or lens doesn't add water.
column29: How can you add water without moving the cover slip?

column9: Read a student's plan: (1) Carry the microscope to the table by the arm with one hand. (2) Plug it in and turn on the light. (3) Place the slide on the stage under the stage clips. (4) Focus on the 4× objective with the coarse knob. Which step should be changed?
column14: Step 2; the light should stay off
column15: Step 1; carry it with one hand on the arm and the other under the base
column16: Step 3; slides don't go under the stage clips, because the clips can scratch them
column17: Step 4; never start on the 4× objective, since it is too weak to show cells
column28: Steps 2 to 4 are correct. Step 1 is risky: a microscope should be carried upright with two hands, one on the arm and one supporting the base, so it can't slip or swing into something.
column29: Check each step for what could go wrong. Which one could lead to a dropped microscope?

column9: A student's onion cells are in focus on 4×, but the cells are almost clear and very hard to see. Which changes could make them easier to see? Choose all that apply.
column14: Close the diaphragm a little to add contrast
column15: Turn the coarse knob all the way down
column16: Add a drop of stain such as iodine
column17: Open the diaphragm all the way
column28: Nearly clear cells are easier to see with less light (more contrast) or with a stain that colors them. Flooding them with more light makes them even harder to see, and the coarse knob and removing the cover slip don't add contrast.
column29: The problem isn't focus; it's that the cells blend in with the background.

column9: The lamp is on and the diaphragm is open, but half of the view is dark, like a half-moon. What is the most likely cause?
column14: The objective lens is not clicked all the way into place
column15: The slide is a prepared slide
column16: The fine knob is turned too far
column28: If the objective is halfway between click stops, it lines up with only part of the light path, so you get a half-dark view. Turn the nosepiece until it clicks. Focus and specimen thickness affect sharpness, not half the field going dark.
column29: What part has a "click" when it lines up correctly?

column9: A magnifying glass magnifies about 5×. A compound light microscope can reach 400× or more. What is the main reason a compound microscope can magnify so much more?
column15: Its stage holds the specimen closer to your eye
column17: Its two lenses each enlarge the image, one after the other
column28: A compound microscope's objective lens makes an enlarged image, and the ocular lens enlarges that image again, so the powers multiply (for example 10 × 40 = 400). Light helps you see, but it doesn't magnify, and the diaphragm only controls brightness.
column29: What does the word compound tell you about the lenses?

column9: With a 10× ocular, which data table is most likely correct?
column14: 4× objective: 40× total, 0.45 mm field; 10×: 100× total, 1.8 mm field; 40×: 400× total, 4.5 mm field
column15: 4× objective: 14× total, 4.5 mm field; 10×: 20× total, 1.8 mm field; 40×: 50× total, 0.45 mm field
column16: 4× objective: 40× total, 4.5 mm field; 10×: 100× total, 1.8 mm field; 40×: 400× total, 0.45 mm field
column17: 4× objective: 40× total, 4.5 mm field; 10×: 100× total, 4.5 mm field; 40×: 400× total, 4.5 mm field
column28: The correct table multiplies to get each total (10 × 4 = 40, and so on) and shows the field of view shrinking as magnification goes up. The other tables have the field growing, totals found by adding, or a field that never changes.
column29: Check two things: are the totals multiplied, and does the field get smaller as you zoom in?
